content: Anaphylaxis Severe and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Patients with a known history of penicillin hypersensitivity have also experienced severe reactions when treated with cephalosporins. Before starting therapy with Bicillin C-R, it is essential to thoroughly investigate any prior hypersensitivity reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other allergens. If an allergic reaction occurs, Bicillin C-R must be discontinued immediately, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. Severe anaphylactic reactions require emergency intervention, including the administration of epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous corticosteroids, and airway management, such as intubation, as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD) Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Bicillin C-R. The severity of CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to life-threatening colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may not respond to antimicrobial therapy and could require surgical intervention, such as colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use, even if symptoms occur up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotics not targeting C. difficile may be necessary. Management should include fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation as needed. Method of Administration Bicillin C-R must not be injected into or near an artery or nerve, as this can result in permanent neurological damage. Accidental intravascular administration, including direct intra-arterial injection or injection near arteries, has caused severe neurovascular complications, such as transverse myelitis with permanent paralysis, gangrene requiring amputation, and tissue necrosis at or near the injection site. These complications have been reported following injections into the buttock, thigh, and deltoid areas. Other serious complications include pallor, mottling, or cyanosis of the extremity, followed by blister formation and severe edema, which may necessitate surgical intervention, such as fasciotomy. These effects are more commonly reported in infants and young children. If there is any evidence of compromised blood supply at or near the injection site, immediate consultation with a specialist is required. Bicillin C-R must not be administered intravenously or mixed with intravenous solutions. Accidental intravenous administration of penicillin G benzathine has been associated with cardiorespiratory arrest and death. Repeated intramuscular injections into the anterolateral thigh have been linked to quadriceps femoris fibrosis and atrophy. General Precautions Bicillin C-R should only be prescribed for confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infections or for prophylactic purposes. Unnecessary use increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Penicillins should be used cautiously in patients with a history of significant allergies or asthma. Care must be taken to avoid intravenous or intra-arterial administration or injection near major peripheral nerves or blood vessels, as these can cause neurovascular damage. A small percentage of patients may be sensitive to procaine. If there is a history of sensitivity, a test dose of 0.1 mL of a 1–2% procaine solution should be administered intradermally. The development of erythema, wheal, flare, or eruption indicates sensitivity, and procaine penicillin preparations should not be used. Procaine sensitivity should be managed with standard treatments, including barbiturates, and antihistamines may be beneficial. Antibiotic use may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms. If allergic reactions occur, penicillin therapy should be stopped unless the condition being treated is life-threatening and no alternative treatment is available. For prolonged or high-dose penicillin therapy, periodic evaluation of renal and hematopoietic systems is recommended. Patient Information Patients should be informed that diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves after discontinuation. However, if watery or bloody stools occur, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even up to two months after completing therapy, they should contact their physician immediately. Patients should also be advised that Bicillin C-R is only effective against bacterial infections and does not treat viral infections, such as the common cold. They should be instructed to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed, even if they feel better early in treatment. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce the effectiveness of treatment and increase the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Laboratory Monitoring In cases of streptococcal infections, therapy must be sufficient to eradicate the organism to prevent complications of streptococcal disease. Post-treatment cultures should be performed to confirm the elimination of streptococci. Pregnancy and Nursing Penicillin G has been classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies in mice, rats, and rabbits have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus or impaired fertility. Human data have not demonstrated adverse effects on the fetus, but there are no well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Therefore, penicillin G should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. Soluble penicillin G is excreted in breast milk, so caution is advised when administering penicillin G benzathine or penicillin G procaine to nursing mothers. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and Fertility No long-term animal studies have been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic or mutagenic potential of these drugs or their effects on fertility. Pediatric Use Refer to the Indications and Usage and Dosage and Administration sections for specific pediatric recommendations. Geriatric Use Clinical studies have not included sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified significant differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. In general, dosing for elderly patients should start at the lower end of the range, reflecting the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of other medical conditions or concurrent drug therapies. Since penicillin G is substantially excreted by the kidneys, the risk of toxic reactions may be higher in patients with impaired renal function. Renal function should be monitored, and dose adjustments may be necessary.
